passages.t: The shaved head and the hair in thirds
passages.happening: God tells Ezekiel to use a sharp sword as a barber's razor and shave his head and beard, then weigh the hair on scales and divide it (verse 1). When the days of the siege are over, he is to burn a third inside the city, strike a third with the sword around it, and scatter a third to the wind (verse 2). He is to keep a few strands in the folds of his garment, and then throw some of those into the fire as well (verses 3-4).
passages.hearers:
Shaving was full of meaning. Shaving the head and beard was a sign of mourning or public disgrace, and the law forbade priests to shave their heads or the edges of their beards. For Ezekiel, a priest, to shave with a sword was to act out humiliation, grief and the collapse of holiness at once. The sword doing the barber's work tells the exiles who the real barber will be: the invading army. Weighing the hair on scales suggests a judgment that is measured, not random.

The few strands kept in his garment picture a remnant, but even some of those are burned. Survival is not automatic.
passages.later: The law said of priests, ‘Priests must not make bald spots on their heads, shave off the edges of their beards, or make cuts in their bodies’ (Leviticus 21:5). Isaiah pictured Assyria as a razor that would shave the land (Isaiah 7:20).
passages.asks: The hair was weighed before it was divided. Ask what it means that God's judgments are measured, not careless. And ask what it means to be among the few strands he keeps.

passages.t: Jerusalem in the center of the nations
passages.happening:
‘This is Jerusalem, which I have set in the center of the nations, with countries all around her’ (verse 5). But she has rebelled against God's ordinances more than the nations around her (verses 6-7). So God says, ‘Behold, I Myself am against you, Jerusalem’ (verse 8). Because the city has defiled his sanctuary with idols, he will not spare it (verse 11).

Verse 10 names the worst horror of a siege, the hunger that drives families against one another; these notes name it and do not describe it. A third of the people will die of plague and famine within the city, a third will fall by the sword outside it, and a third will be scattered (verse 12). Then God's anger will be spent, ‘they will know that I, the LORD, in My zeal have spoken’ (verse 13), and the city will become a warning to the nations (verses 14-17).
passages.hearers:
These were the real fates of ancient sieges: disease and hunger inside the walls, slaughter of those who fled or fought, and deportation of the survivors. Lamentations and 2 Kings record the same after Jerusalem fell.

The terrible hunger of verse 10 was not invented by Ezekiel. The covenant curses had warned of it, an earlier siege of Samaria saw it, and Lamentations grieves that it happened in Jerusalem.

Many peoples believed their holy city stood at the center of the world. God grants that Jerusalem was set in the center of the nations, and turns the privilege into the ground of her accountability.
passages.later: The covenant had warned of siege famine in the plainest terms (Leviticus 26:29; Deuteronomy 28:53). Lamentations grieves that it came to pass (Lamentations 4:10).
passages.hard:
How can God say he will not pity or spare, and that his wrath will be spent, without seeming cruel?

The difficulty is real, and the language is severe on purpose. Several things help in reading it honestly. This is covenant speech: Israel had bound itself to God with promises and curses spelled out in advance, and the prophets had warned for generations. The wrath is not a loss of temper but a judgment on wrongs the text names, chiefly idolatry and the defiling of the temple. And the phrase about wrath being spent implies that judgment has a limit and an end; the book goes on to promise restoration (chapters 11, 36 and 37).

Some readers still find these images too dark to reconcile with a loving God, and the book does not soften them. Its answer is that sin against a holy God is terribly serious, and that his final purpose is not destruction but a people who know him. This is Israel's own Scripture, spoken by an Israelite prophet to his own people. It is no key to anyone's suffering now, and it is never a reason to blame the Jewish people.
passages.asks: Jerusalem's privilege made her more accountable, not less. Ask what privileges you have been given in faith. And ask what responsibility comes with them.
